analysis.one_liner: Lets workers divert a share of their Social Security payroll taxes into private investment accounts.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate's closing weeks by retiring Sen. Phil Gramm, the bill was referred to the Finance Committee and died there without a hearing, markup, or vote before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have let workers born in 1953 or later choose to divert part of their Social Security payroll taxes — starting at about 3.1 percent of wages and potentially rising to 8 percent — into personal investment accounts ("SAFE accounts") run by government-certified funds. At retirement, most of the account would be converted into an annuity from a certified fund, with a 20 percent bonus on top of the promised traditional benefit, and the government guaranteed that no electing worker would receive less than the benefit promised under the current program. The bill capped fund fees at 0.3 percent of assets, exempted the accounts' investment earnings from corporate income tax, created a new Social Security Investment Board to certify and regulate the funds, and eventually would have cut payroll tax rates for both workers and employers. It was introduced in the final weeks of the 107th Congress by retiring Sen. Phil Gramm, referred to the Finance Committee, and never received any hearing, vote, or further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers born in 1953 or later who elect the new option would own accounts holding a share of their payroll taxes, with any market gains theirs to keep (including amounts inheritable by family), a 20 percent bonus on top of promised benefits at retirement, and a federal guarantee they never fall below the traditional benefit. Employers and workers would eventually see payroll tax rates cut once the account investment rate reaches 8 percent. The financial industry gains the most structurally: certified funds would administer a new stream of contributions with capped but guaranteed fees, and annuity providers would sell SAFER annuities to every retiring account holder.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Opting workers; certified fund and annuity firms

how_it_helps.text: Workers born in 1953 or later could elect to have a share of their payroll taxes (a base rate starting at 3.1 percent of wages, potentially rising to 8 percent) deposited into a SAFE Account they own, invested through certified funds.

The bill guarantees that electing workers receive a total monthly benefit no lower than what current law promises, topped up from the trust fund if their annuity falls short, and lets workers reject the new system at retirement and take full traditional benefits instead.

Account balances would be the sole property of the worker, with any remaining assets after buying an annuity payable to the worker, and balances at death going to family or the worker's estate — unlike traditional Social Security benefits.

Administrative fees are capped at 0.3 percent of assets, funds must accept all applicants and charge uniform fees, and every worker of the same age must get the same monthly benefit regardless of sex, race, or health status.

analysis.who_pays: If enacted, the trust funds would lose payroll revenue to the accounts in the near term, and the bill draws account contributions, the corporate-tax exemption, and trust fund reimbursement from federal budget surpluses and trust fund surplus income — so taxpayers and the existing system bear the transition cost. The federal guarantee means any shortfalls in workers' accounts are made up from the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund. Covered employers take on new payroll-administration duties for account designations and reporting.

drawbacks.text: Diverting a share of payroll contributions into SAFE Accounts would have drained revenue from the trust funds that pay current beneficiaries, worsening the system's near-term financing even as the bill promised long-term savings.

The guarantee of never falling below the promised benefit is backstopped by the Federal Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund, meaning any worker whose investments underperform would draw guaranty payments from the same trust fund the accounts had drained.

The plan depends on money that may not exist: account contributions, the corporate-tax exemption, and trust fund reimbursement are all drawn from budget or trust fund surpluses, and the bill's own corporate-tax recapture rests on assumed percentages (80 percent of account assets as a net addition to national investment, taxed at an assumed effective 23.9 percent) rather than actual receipts.
The bill exempts SAFE Account and SAFER Annuity investment earnings from federal corporate income taxes, reducing federal revenue and concentrating a further tax advantage with certified funds.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real potential upside for younger workers: personally owned, inheritable accounts, investment returns historically higher than the trust fund's government bonds, and a federal guarantee that no one would fall below the promised benefit. But the costs were serious and the design strained the numbers: diverting up to 8 percent of payroll into private accounts removed revenue the system needs to pay current beneficiaries, the federal guarantee turned market losses into a public obligation, and the bill leaned on budget surpluses — of the kind that existed in the late 1990s but were disappearing in 2002 — to plug the gap. Independent analysts of similar carve-out plans generally found that the transition costs, not benefit improvements, dominated. Whether the trade was worth it was exactly the debate the bill never got to have: it died in committee without a hearing, cost estimate, or vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and sat there until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 19, 2002, in the Senate's post-election session, read twice, and referred to the Committee on Finance.
The complete action history shows no further action: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, and no companion House action before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.
Besides sponsor Sen. Phil Gramm, only one senator cosponsored the bill, giving it one of the smallest sponsorship bases of any major Social Security proposal in the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing Social Security system stayed exactly as it was: no worker's account, benefit, or payroll tax changed. The financial and annuity industries did not gain the new certified-fund business the bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The existing Social Security system, unchanged

for.name: Sen. Phil Gramm
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the final weeks of the 107th Congress and authored its private-account structure.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Hagel
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor.

for.name: President George W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Publicly championed personal retirement accounts as the fix for Social Security's financing, including through his 2001 commission on Social Security reform, giving the bill's approach White House-level advocacy.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (chaired by Max Baucus)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral: no hearing, no markup, no vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored only by two Republicans and died in committee without any roll-call votes or floor debate, so the record shows no partisan split to measure.

industries.note: The bill makes certified funds the permanent channel for a share of every electing worker's Social Security contributions, with a guaranteed stream of new assets and a fee cap of 0.3 percent of assets per year — government-certified, uniform-fee business that workers cannot receive outside the new system.

Retiring workers would be required to convert most of their account into a SAFER annuity bought from a certified annuity fund, creating a large mandatory annuity market with guaranteed acceptance and capped fees.

Covered employers would handle account designations on W-4 forms and report contributions on W-2 statements, adding payroll administration work; the bill directs the Investment Board to minimize that burden.
